Geostatistics and spatial epidemiology

Source: vignettes/geostatistics-and-epidemiology.Rmd
geostatistics-and-epidemiology.Rmd

Variograms and kriging, and area-level models of rates with spatial dependence.

Each section is one help page: what the function is for, the example of its help page as it runs, and the plot of its result where the package draws one. ?name gives the arguments and the value in full.

Geostatistics

Empirical semivariogram

vgemp(): The classical estimator of Matheron (1963): half the mean squared difference of the values over the pairs of points whose distance falls in each of nbins equal bins of (0, cutoff] (the first bin closed at 0). Bins without pairs are left out. The semivariogram describes how dissimilar values become with distance, the first step of kriging: rates of a crime, a disease or a survey outcome measured at places.

# simulated values with a trend from west to east
set.seed(1)
p <- cbind(x = runif(60, 0, 10), y = runif(60, 0, 10))
v <- p[, 1] * 0.5 + rnorm(60, 0, 0.3)
vgemp(p, v = v)
#>         dist      gamma np
#> 1  0.3883710 0.03235575 14
#> 2  0.6472850 0.10202814 16
#> 3  0.9061991 0.14740942 25
#> 4  1.1651131 0.17579384 27
#> 5  1.4240271 0.12605216 28
#> 6  1.6829411 0.20833025 43
#> 7  1.9418551 0.27639636 43
#> 8  2.2007691 0.37523216 57
#> 9  2.4596831 0.46234587 48
#> 10 2.7185972 0.54284954 60
#> 11 2.9775112 0.68058945 69
#> 12 3.2364252 0.78158842 69
#> 13 3.4953392 0.74873781 60
#> 14 3.7542532 0.84625342 76

Fit a variogram model by Gaussian maximum likelihood

vgfit(): Fits the nugget, partial sill and range of a spherical, exponential or Gaussian covariance model by maximising the Gaussian log-likelihood of the values about a constant mean (Mardia and Marshall 1984). The search is the Nelder-Mead simplex of R’s optim() (at most 800 evaluations) on the logarithms of the three parameters, from 0.1 and 0.9 of the variance of the values and a quarter of the largest distance. The covariance matrix gets 1e-8 of the variance on its diagonal so that it stays positive definite.

set.seed(1)
p <- cbind(x = runif(40, 0, 10), y = runif(40, 0, 10))
v <- p[, 1] * 0.5 + rnorm(40, 0, 0.3)
vgfit(p, v = v)
#> vgfit: exponential model by maximum likelihood
#>       nugget        psill        range       loglik 
#>  0.006099213  8.719291632 71.862753310 11.408010219

Ordinary kriging

okrge(): Predicts the values at new locations at by ordinary kriging: the best linear unbiased predictor under a variogram model with an unknown constant mean (Cressie 1993, sec. 3.2), with its kriging variance. The variogram is vgm, a list such as vgfit() returns; without it, an exponential model is fitted by weighted least squares to the 15-bin vgemp() semivariogram with the weights np / h^2 of Cressie (1985), which is fast but rougher than vgfit().

set.seed(1)
p <- cbind(x = runif(60), y = runif(60))
v <- sin(3 * p[, 1]) + rnorm(60, sd = 0.1)
okrge(p, v = v, at = cbind(0.5, 0.5))
#>      pred        var
#> 1 1.06704 0.01030984
okrge(p, v = v, at = cbind(0.5, 0.5),
      vgm = list(model = "exponential", nugget = 0.01, psill = 0.3,
                 range = 0.4))
#>       pred        var
#> 1 1.062215 0.04918238

Ordinary block kriging

bkrig(): Predicts the mean value over each block (an area such as a district) by ordinary kriging with point-to-block covariances averaged over the block, C(s_i, B) = (1 / |B|) int_B C(s_i, u) du, under the exponential covariance (sill - nugget) exp(-h / range), plus nugget at distance 0 (Schabenberger and Gotway 2005, ch. 4). A block is a box, given as a 2 x 2 matrix of its lower and upper corners (rows) and integrated on a regular grid of round(sqrt(nq))^2 points, or a matrix of the points that discretise it.

set.seed(1)
p <- cbind(x = runif(30), y = runif(30))
v <- p[, 1] + rnorm(30, sd = 0.1)
bkrig(p, v = v, blocks = list(rbind(c(0, 0), c(0.5, 0.5)),
                              rbind(c(0.5, 0.5), c(1, 1))),
      range = 0.3)
#>         est        se
#> 1 0.3357770 0.1852905
#> 2 0.7159535 0.2114923

Leave-one-out cross-validation of ordinary kriging

krigcv(): Predicts each value from all the others by ordinary kriging with the exponential covariance of bkrig(), and summarises the residuals by the mean squared prediction error MSPE = (1 / n) sum (Z(s_i) - Z_-i(s_i))^2, its root and the mean absolute error (Schabenberger and Gotway 2005, ch. 4). Comparing it across covariance parameters chooses among them.

set.seed(1)
p <- cbind(x = runif(30), y = runif(30))
krigcv(p, v = rnorm(30), range = 0.2)
#> krigcv: leave-one-out kriging of 30 values
#>      mspe     rmspe       mae 
#> 0.7067174 0.8406648 0.7098562

Polynomial trend surface

trsurf(): Fits the mean of the values as a polynomial in the coordinates by ordinary least squares, mu(s) = sum_k beta_k f_k(s), the f_k the monomials up to degree order: 1; x, y; x2, y2, xy; x3, y3, x2y, xy2 (Schabenberger and Gotway 2005, ch. 2). The large- scale trend is often removed this way before a variogram is fitted to the residuals.

set.seed(1)
p <- cbind(x = runif(50), y = runif(50))
v <- 1 + 2 * p[, 1] - p[, 2]^2 + rnorm(50, sd = 0.1)
f <- trsurf(p, v = v)
f
#> trsurf: trend surface of order 2 on 50 points, R-squared 0.9818
#>           1           x           y          x2          y2          xy 
#>  1.09625518  2.11305475 -0.73267272 -0.08022062 -0.33750250  0.14443429
summary(f)
#>   term         est         se          z
#> 1    1  1.09625518 0.07968901 13.7566670
#> 2    x  2.11305475 0.21086371 10.0209505
#> 3    y -0.73267272 0.25326074 -2.8929581
#> 4   x2 -0.08022062 0.18258998 -0.4393484
#> 5   y2 -0.33750250 0.21097762 -1.5997076
#> 6   xy  0.14443429 0.18005051  0.8021877

Spatial linear model by profile maximum likelihood

sglmx(): The Gaussian spatial linear model v = Z beta + delta + e, delta a Gaussian process with covariance sigma2 exp(-h / phi), without a nugget (Schabenberger and Gotway 2005, ch. 5). The range phi is found by maximising the profile likelihood with Brent’s method on log(phi) over [log(max(h / 100, 0.001)), log(max(3 h, 1))], h the largest distance, as R’s optimize() runs it; beta follows by generalised least squares. The standard errors use sigma2 estimated with n - p degrees of freedom.

set.seed(1)
p <- cbind(x = runif(40), y = runif(40))
z <- cbind(1, p[, 1])
sglmx(1 + 2 * p[, 1] + rnorm(40, sd = 0.2), z, p)
#> sglmx: spatial linear model, exponential covariance, 40 points
#>         z1         z2     sigma2        phi 
#> 0.97349153 2.09618531 0.03478370 0.01495528

Spatial linear mixed model by REML

smixm(): The model v = Z beta + delta + e, delta ~ N(0, sigma2 R_phi) with the exponential correlation R_phi = exp(-h / phi) and a nugget e ~ N(0, tau2 I), tau2 = nu sigma2, by restricted maximum likelihood (Patterson and Thompson 1971; Schabenberger and Gotway 2005, ch. 5). The search is R’s Nelder-Mead (optim(), 400 evaluations, relative tolerance 1e-6) on (log phi, log nu) from (log(h / 3), log(0.1)), h the largest distance (at least 1).

set.seed(1)
p <- cbind(x = runif(40), y = runif(40))
smixm(1 + 2 * p[, 1] + rnorm(40, sd = 0.3), cbind(1, p[, 1]), p)
#> smixm: spatial linear mixed model by REML, 40 points
#>         z1         z2     sigma2       tau2        phi 
#> 0.96148075 2.14380681 0.06465755 0.01544588 0.03247176

A spatial data object

spobj(): Holds points with their attributes and their coordinate reference system: the coordinates come from two columns of a data frame, the other columns are kept as attributes. The system is an EPSG code, never a PROJ string: 4326 (WGS 84 longitude and latitude, in degrees), 3857 (Web Mercator, in metres) or another code, taken to be in metres. spxy() returns the coordinates, crsof() the system, lfspec() the specification of a web map and spsamp() a sample of the points.

d <- data.frame(lon = c(-79.4, -79.3), lat = c(43.6, 43.7), v = c(1, 2))
s <- spobj(d, c("lon", "lat"))
s
#> spobj: 2 points, EPSG:4326 (degrees)
format(s)
#> [1] "spobj: 2 points, EPSG:4326 (degrees)"
summary(s)
#>   coord   min   max
#> 1   lon -79.4 -79.3
#> 2   lat  43.6  43.7

The coordinates of a spatial data object

spxy(): The coordinates of a spatial data object

spxy(spobj(data.frame(lon = 1:3, lat = 1:3)))
#>      lon lat
#> [1,]   1   1
#> [2,]   2   2
#> [3,]   3   3

The coordinate reference system of a spatial data object

crsof(): Gives the system as its EPSG code and a label in the style of WKT2, never as a PROJ string.

crsof(spobj(data.frame(lon = 1, lat = 1)))
#> $epsg
#> [1] 4326
#> 
#> $wkt
#> [1] "GEOGCRS[\"WGS 84\", EPSG:4326]"

The specification of a web map

lfspec(): Describes an interactive map of the points as data, for a mapping library to draw: the tile provider, the centre (the mean longitude and latitude), a zoom level and the points in longitude and latitude. Web Mercator coordinates (EPSG:3857) are taken back to longitude and latitude by the inverse of the spherical Mercator projection.

lfspec(spobj(data.frame(lon = c(-79.4, -79.3), lat = c(43.6, 43.7))))
#> $provider
#> [1] "OpenStreetMap"
#> 
#> $interactive
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $center
#>    lon    lat 
#> -79.35  43.65 
#> 
#> $zoom
#> [1] 8
#> 
#> $points
#>        lon  lat
#> [1,] -79.4 43.6
#> [2,] -79.3 43.7

Sample points, by local density or uniformly

spsamp(): Draws size of the points without replacement. With dens = TRUE each draw picks a point with probability proportional to its local density sum_j exp(-(d_ij / b)^2), b the median distance between points (great-circle distance for EPSG:4326), so that dense areas are sampled more; otherwise every point is equally likely.

s <- spobj(expand.grid(lon = 1:5, lat = 1:5))
spsamp(s, 5, seed = 1)
#> [1]  8 20 10  6 18
#> attr(,"prob")
#>  [1] 0.02813274 0.03613227 0.03913468 0.03613227 0.02813274 0.03614678 0.04642113
#>  [8] 0.05027751 0.04642113 0.03614678 0.03916871 0.05029579 0.05447252 0.05029579
#> [15] 0.03916871 0.03618351 0.04645522 0.05031121 0.04645522 0.03618351 0.02818869
#> [22] 0.03618420 0.03918600 0.03618420 0.02818869

Spatial epidemiology

Bayes outbreak detection

bayout(): The Bayes detector of surveillance::algo.bayes() (Riebler 2004; Hoehle 2007) for a series of counts: at each time t the reference counts are the w before it (acty = TRUE) and, in each of the b years before, the 2 w + 1 counts around the same time of year (freq counts per year); missing counts are left out. With s their sum and n their number, the posterior predictive distribution of the count at t under a Poisson model with a flat prior is negative binomial of size s + 0.5 and probability n / (n + 1); its 1 - alpha quantile is the upper bound, and a count above it raises an alarm. The same series may be calls for service, emergency visits or reported crimes of one kind.

bayout(c(3, 5, 2, 4, 6, 3, 4, 12), w = 6, at = 8)
#>   t ub alarm
#> 1 8  8  TRUE

Exposure within a buffer

bufexp(): For each receptor (a home, a school), the number of sources (bars, polluting sites, hot spots) within distance r, their summed weights and the distance to the nearest: the buffer measure of exposure assessment. Distances are planar, or great-circle metres when lonlat = TRUE (the coordinates then longitude and latitude in degrees).

rec <- cbind(x = c(0, 1, 5), y = c(0, 1, 5))
src <- cbind(x = c(0.5, 4), y = c(0.5, 4))
bufexp(rec, src = src, r = 1.5)
#>   count wsum      near
#> 1     1    1 0.7071068
#> 2     1    1 0.7071068
#> 3     1    1 1.4142136

Exposure by kernel

kerexp(): The kernel-weighted density of sources at each receptor, sum_j w_j K(d_ij / h) / h^2, with the bivariate normal kernel exp(-u^2 / 2) / (2 pi) or the quartic kernel 3 / pi (1 - u^2)^2 (for u < 1, 0 beyond) of Bailey and Gatrell (1995). Planar coordinates.

kerexp(rbind(c(0.2, 0.3)), src = rbind(c(0.25, 0.35), c(0.6, 0.8)),
       h = 0.5, kern = "quartic")
#> [1] 3.668458

The Leroux precision matrix

lerprc(): The precision of the area effects in the model of Leroux, Lei and Breslow (2000), tau (rho Q + (1 - rho) I), with Q = D - W the Laplacian of the neighbour weights: independent effects at rho = 0, the intrinsic conditional autoregression at rho = 1.

lerprc(rbind(c(0, 1, 0), c(1, 0, 1), c(0, 1, 0)), 0.5, 2)
#>      [,1] [,2] [,3]
#> [1,]    2   -1    0
#> [2,]   -1    3   -1
#> [3,]    0   -1    2

The BYM2 area structure

bym2sc(): The scaled structure of the BYM2 model of Riebler et al. (2016): the generalised inverse G of the Laplacian Q of the neighbour weights (from its eigenvalues above tol times the largest), the scaling factor s, the geometric mean of the diagonal of G, so that the structured effect has a generalised variance of 1, and the covariance of the area effects ((1 - phi) I + phi G / s) / tau. The graph must be connected and every area must have a neighbour.

w <- rbind(c(0, 1, 1, 0), c(1, 0, 1, 0), c(1, 1, 0, 1), c(0, 0, 1, 0))
bym2sc(w, 2, 0.4)$scale
#> [1] 0.3565926

Ecological regression with expected counts

ecolrg(): Regression of area counts y on covariates with the offset log(e), e the expected counts (from indirect standardisation, say), so that the coefficients act on the standardised ratio: Poisson by iteratively reweighted least squares; negative binomial, alternating Newton steps on the score of theta with reweighted fits of the coefficients; or zero-inflated Poisson (Lambert 1992) by EM, the zero part logistic on an intercept and the columns of z.

# simulated counts and expected counts
set.seed(1)
x <- rnorm(30)
e <- runif(30, 3, 8)
y <- rpois(30, e * exp(0.2 + 0.4 * x))
ecolrg(y, e, x)
#> ecolrg: 30 counts, log-likelihood -67.3106
#> [1] 0.1404659 0.4851843

Eigenvector spatial filtering

evfilt(): Adds Moran eigenvectors of the neighbour weights to the regression of v on an intercept and x by forward selection, so that the residuals lose their spatial autocorrelation (Griffith 2003; Tiefelsdorf and Griffith 2007). The Moran eigenvectors are the eigenvectors of the symmetrised weights (W + W’) / 2 orthogonal to the constant (computed in the Helmert basis), each with Moran’s I n / S0 lambda; the candidates are those with Moran’s I above -1 / (n - 1) ("positive", the usual choice), below it, or all. Selection by method: "moran" takes the vector that most reduces the absolute residual Moran’s I until it is below tol; "aic" and "press" (the leave-one-out prediction error) while they fall; "r2" while R-squared rises by tol or more. At least two residual degrees of freedom are kept.

w <- 1 * (abs(outer(1:8, 1:8, "-")) == 1)
v <- c(1, 2, 2.5, 4, 3.5, 3, 1.5, 1)
evfilt(v, w, method = "aic")
#> evfilt: 1 eigenvectors selected, residual Moran's I -0.7032, R-squared 0.9199

The metapopulation SIR model

spsir(): The deterministic SIR model on patches (Keeling and Rohani 2008, sec. 7.3): the force of infection on patch i is beta sum_j C_ij I_j / N_j with the coupling C = (1 - kappa) I + kappa W~, W~ the row-standardised neighbour weights, so that a share kappa of the pressure comes from neighbours; recovery is at rate gamma. Integrated by the classical fourth-order Runge-Kutta method in steps of dt. The same equations describe the spread of an outbreak of violence between neighbourhoods in contagion models.

w <- rbind(c(0, 1, 0), c(1, 0, 1), c(0, 1, 0))
spsir(c(10, 0, 0), w, rep(1000, 3), beta = 0.6, gamma = 0.2,
      tmax = 60, dt = 0.5)
#> spsir: 3 patches to time 60, attack rate 0.9399, R0 3

Spatial frailty and cure models

sfrail(), sfcure(): sfrail() fits the Weibull proportional hazards model with log-frailties of the areas under an intrinsic conditional autoregression, h(t) = rho t^(rho - 1) exp(x beta + u_area) (Banerjee, Wall and Carlin 2003); sfcure() the promotion-time cure model (Chen, Ibrahim and Sinha 1999), S(t) = exp(-theta (1 - exp(-G(t)))), theta = exp(x beta + u_area) and G(t) = exp(c + rho log t), whose cure fraction is exp(-theta). Both maximise the penalised likelihood, the penalty tau u’Qu / 2 with Q the Laplacian of the neighbour weights, by Newton-Raphson from 0 on the analytic gradient with a Hessian by central differences, the step halved while the objective falls, until a step is below tol (200 iterations at most). The standard errors come from the last Hessian; the first is that of the log shape.

# simulated survival times in three areas
w <- rbind(c(0, 1, 0), c(1, 0, 1), c(0, 1, 0))
i <- 0:29
x <- sin(i)
t <- 0.5 + ((i * 7) %% 11) / 5 * exp(-0.5 * x - 0.3 * (i %% 3))
f <- sfrail(t, as.numeric(i %% 5 != 0), x, i %% 3 + 1, w)
f
#> sfrail: Weibull frailty model, shape 3.065, penalised log-likelihood -20.2083
#> [1]  0.9000010 -1.9361730 -1.2253279 -0.8237804
summary(f)
#>       term        est        se         z
#> 1 logshape  1.1201896 0.1648807  6.793941
#> 2       x1  0.9000010 0.3560158  2.527981
#> 3   frail1 -1.9361730 0.4750970 -4.075321
#> 4   frail2 -1.2253279 0.4050962 -3.024783
#> 5   frail3 -0.8237804 0.3803217 -2.166009

The spatial encoding of graph attention

spbias(): Turns a matrix of hop distances between the nodes of a network (areas, places, people) into the bias that Graphormer (Ying et al. 2021) adds to the attention logits: a learnable value per distance, b[d + 1] (the last for every larger distance), and ub for pairs that cannot reach each other (distance -1). A bias inside the softmax keeps distant nodes reachable but discouraged.

d <- rbind(c(0, 1, 2), c(1, 0, -1), c(2, -1, 0))
spbias(d, b = c(1, 0.5, 0.25))
#> $bias
#>      [,1]  [,2]   [,3]
#> [1,] 1.00   0.5   0.25
#> [2,] 0.50   1.0 -10.00
#> [3,] 0.25 -10.0   1.00
#> 
#> $ub
#> [1] -10
